children: The European Union's proposal on Wednesday to make Canada its first "associate member" ahead of Prime Minister Mark Carney's speech to the EU Parliament Thursday could aggravate the spat between the U.S. and Canada.

Both Canada and the EU have been trying to shore up relationships with countries other than the U.S. as tensions with the Trump administration have flared-on trade as well as on broader issues. Canada is in the midst of a trade tit-for-tat with the U.S. following a breakdown in talks last month. The U.S. has banned alcohol and other imports from Canada, increased tariffs, and provoked questions about whether it will renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade pact, which underpins a trade relationship that is critical for both countries.

For now, the EU's invitation is more symbolic than substantial. Canada is not eligible to join the EU since it's not physically on the continent. And BCA Research's Matt Gertken notes that Canada would have no interest in diluting its sovereignty, a prerequisite for EU membership.

While the EU's move is not certain to trigger another batch of retaliatory measures from the Trump administration, Eurasia Group's Graeme Thompson says it could be perceived in Washington as a poke-much the same as Carney's call for middle powers to unite at Davos earlier this year was. Invoking something "that doesn't actually exist nor is likely to be created," says Thompson, could fan the flames of the spat between the two neighbors rather than throw cooling water on the fire.

In substance, the EU-Canada proposal is about deepening and broadening trade and collaboration on critical minerals. That could bring greater attention to a recurring European-Canadian summit next month, which typically would not register on most radars. Thompson expects the summit to be more ambitious this time, highlighting critical minerals, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, and aerospace and defense as areas for deeper cooperation.

Canada and the EU still rely heavily on U.S. market access, and the EU has to be careful that any additional benefits it grants Canada won't set off a range of claims from Switzerland, the U.K., and others, says Christopher Smart, founder of consultancy Arbroath Group and a former Treasury official.

Still, the proposal for associate membership sends a powerful signal as countries try to navigate growing demands from the U.S. and China, and it is a way for Canada's Carney and the EU's Ursula von der Leyen to assert a degree of independence from President Donald Trump's America First strategy, Smart says. "It's intended as a signal that they have options now that Washington is playing a much more selfish game on trade," he adds.
Investors might want to wait to see how it lands in Washington to gauge whether it could be tinder for more trade and economic volatility.
